newsitem.title: USA: C.R. Bard reorganizing, may see Q3 charge.
newsitem.headline: C.R. Bard reorganizing, may see Q3 charge.

text.p: C.R. Bard Inc Chairman William Longfield said on Wednesday the company was in the process of implementing a series of strategic initatives and it might take an unspecified, one-time third quarter charge.

"We will probably take a write-off in the third quarter related to manufacturing organization," Longfield told a Dillon Read analysts meeting. "We're looking at saving $40 million to $50 million in the cost of goods."

C.R. Bard, which makes and sells health care products, was aiming to reorganize business around three disease areas, take a global management focus, reduce manufacturing and general and administrative costs, boost research and development and divest business which did not grow, he said.

"We are in the middle of implementing these strategies," Longfield said. "We have identified commercial and manufacturing expenses, we are preparing to reduce our eight distribution centers in Europe to one center."
Earnings would feel the benefit of these changes by 1999, Longfield said.
C.R. Bard's business would focus on vascular diagnosis and intervention, oncological diagnosis and intervention and urological diagnosis and intervention, he said.
Growth in the vascular segment would come from both coronary and carotid stents, while within urology, there were big opportunities in the incontinence market, Longfield said.
C.R. Bard's new bladder cancer detection device would also drive top-line growth in the oncology area, he said.
As for non-core business, Longfield said C.R. Bard had targeted roughly $100 million in underperforming assets, and so far had sold about $35 million to $40 million of them.

He said without these assets, the company's sales could grow by as much as nine or ten percent annually, and with the strategic steps, gross margins could rise to between 54 percent and 55 percent from 51 percent.
The company also hoped to take at least one percent out of commercial expenses going forward, Longfield said.
Funds received from the divested businesses would be used to repay debt or buy back stock, he said.
"We hope to get our debt ratio down to between 30 percent and 32 percent over the next few years," Longfield said.
